basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Sensitive topic (student mental health / suicide prevention): informative, supportive framing used throughout; the mortality statistic is stated once, respectfully, without graphic detail, and every slide from Part 3 onward points toward concrete help; the talk closes on the 1925 hotline number and an encouraging, agency-focused message. Facts and sources: 23.1% of university students showed depressive-emotion tendencies in a 2024 survey (June-Oct 2024, n=3,264) by the Counseling Psychologists Association, R.O.C. (中華民國諮商心理師公會全國聯合會); academic pressure and financial difficulty were the top-cited stress sources, future-planning pressure ranked highest across all year levels, third-year students reported the highest overall stress (Heho健康 2024 coverage; epochtimes.com 2024-12-22 report of the same survey). One university (National Chung Cheng University) staff-reported rise from ~6% to ~8-9% with clear depressive symptoms over a decade, used as one illustrative, attributed data point, not a national figure (ccu.edu.tw news page). MOHW mortality data: self-harm is the #2 leading cause of death among Taiwanese aged 15-24 (~25%), and the #1 cause of death for young women in that age band (~34.4%), as reported via the same ccu.edu.tw article citing MOHW statistics -- stated once, respectfully, no method/graphic detail. Student Guidance Law (學生輔導法) revised to move the required university student-to-professional-counselor ratio from 1:1200 to 1:900; MOE began adjusting subsidy budgets from Jan 2024; ~216 additional counseling positions estimated needed nationwide (udn.com 2024 and 2025 coverage). Retention problem: campus counselor positions often pay only ~NT$44,000/month on one-year contracts, making them hard to fill even when funded (twreporter.org, "大專心理師耗竭前的SOS"). Access gap: ~78.5% of students who might benefit do not use their campus counseling center, citing lack of time, distance, and privacy concerns (Heho健康, "大學生心理諮商需求高"). Psychological leave (心理假) exists at many Taiwanese universities but only ~7.5% of students have ever used it (epochtimes.com 2024 report, and ccu.edu.tw). 1925 hotline (依舊愛我): MOHW-run, free, 24/7, single number since Dec 2019 (previously 0800-788-995); documented call volume grew from 27,926 calls (2005) to 78,108 calls (2018, ~6,500/month), reaching ~8,000 calls/month by 2019 -- described in the script only as "has grown steadily for years," not with an unverified recent-year total (mohw.gov.tw hotline history pages). Stigma/help-seeking context: a national adolescent survey (兒福聯盟) found ~39% of youth who struggle emotionally tell no one, correlated with perceived stigma -- used as general context for why stigma, not only access, is part of the problem (udn.com 2024 coverage of 兒福聯盟 survey). No specific 2023-2025 hotline call total was found and confirmed, so none is stated as a precise figure. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: Look around this room for a moment. About one in four students here may feel more stress than they show. That is not a guess, because surveys tell us so.
slides.2: SDG 3 is the goal for good health and well-being. It is not only about the body. It also means care for the mind too. Taiwan takes both parts seriously.
slides.3: University life can look easy from the outside. Classes, clubs and friends fill your schedule every day. But under the surface, many students carry a heavy weight.
slides.4: Here is a real number. In a 2024 survey, 23.1 percent of university students showed signs of depression. That share has grown over the past ten years.
slides.5: Where does this stress come from? Most students point to school and money. Older students feel it the most, right before they must plan their future.
slides.6: Here is a hard fact. Among people aged 15 to 24, self-harm is now the second leading cause of death. This is why the rest of this talk matters.
slides.7: Good news: the law has changed. Schools must now have one counselor for every 900 students, not 1,200. That means more trained help for students like you.
slides.8: Please remember one number: 1925. It is a free hotline, open all day and all night, every day of the year. Someone is always there to listen.
slides.9: Many schools now offer a program called psychological leave. It lets a stressed student take real time off, without shame. That option exists, right now, on your campus.
slides.10: The new law sounds simple: hire more counselors. But schools need real money to pay them well. Without that money, the new rule stays just words on paper.
slides.11: Help should not be hard to find. Instead of one fixed office hour, universities could offer evening slots, online chat, or a quiet drop-in room. Easier access saves lives.
slides.12: Instead of waiting for a crisis, schools can act early. Classes can teach students to notice stress in themselves and their friends. Small lessons now can prevent big pain later.
slides.13: Here is the problem. If schools cannot fill these new counselor jobs, the better ratio only exists on paper. Low pay and short contracts make this job hard to keep.
slides.14: More counselors are not the whole answer. Many people still stay away, even when help is right there. They worry about time, distance, or simply being seen.
slides.15: Psychological leave exists at many schools. Yet only about 7.5 percent of students have ever used it. A right on paper is not the same as a right people use.
slides.16: So we have two gaps, not one. Schools need enough trained staff, and students need to feel safe asking for help. Closing only one gap will not be enough.
slides.17: Let's look at where we stand. Taiwan has a better law, a free hotline, and real leave rules. But staffing and stigma still hold this progress back.
slides.18: You do not need a perfect system to help someone today. If a friend seems different, ask how they really are. That question can matter more than you think.
slides.19: Learn to notice the early signs: less sleep, low energy, or pulling back from friends. Then remember one number, 1925, and say it out loud. It could help someone you love.
slides.20: It is not weakness to ask for help. It is strength, and help exists right now, totally free. If you need it, call 1925, day or night.
